references.text: The Egyptians regarded eating together with Hebrews as an abomination, which shows the cultural and religious contrasts between these groups.
All shepherds were an abomination to the Egyptians, which explains why the Israelites' sacrifice of sheep and goats would provoke them.
Moses warns the Israelites to avoid the abominations of idols, highlighting the contrast between the Lord's offerings and pagan practices.
The Israelites were not to worship the Lord in the same way that the nations worshipped their gods, because the practices of the nations were abominations.
God commanded Moses to ask Pharaoh to let the people travel three days into the wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord, which is the background for this conversation.
Moses insists that they must take their livestock with them to sacrifice to the Lord, and that they do not know what will be needed until they arrive.
Direct narrative connection: 8:22 explains the need for their own sacrificial animals, while 10:25 shows Pharaoh's demand that they bring these along.
Thematic parallel: The fear that foreigners' reaction (mockery or violence) will prevent God's people from serving God rightly.
Theological contrast: The people want to return to Egyptian slavery (14:12), while Moses insists they must offer something the Egyptians detest in order to serve God (8:22).
